questions.stem: In a model of eukaryotic DNA, what holds the two strands of the double helix together?
options: Peptide bonds between sugar molecules on opposite strands
Covalent bonds joining each base to the base opposite it
Phosphodiester bonds joining the two phosphate backbones
Hydrogen bonds between complementary nitrogenous bases
questions.explanation: Complementary bases (A with T, C with G) are held together by hydrogen bonds, which are weak enough for the strands to separate during transcription. Phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides along one strand, not across the helix.

questions.stem: How is DNA packaged inside the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell?
options: It is stored as short single strands bound to ribosomes
It is wound around histone proteins to form chromatin
It is folded into one circular loop free in the nucleus
It is enclosed in a protein capsid on the nuclear membrane
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic DNA is linear and coiled around histone proteins, forming chromatin that condenses further into chromosomes. A single circular loop free in the cell is typical of prokaryotes, not the eukaryotic nucleus.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares mRNA with DNA?
options: mRNA is single-stranded and contains ribose and uracil
mRNA is double-stranded and contains deoxyribose and uracil
mRNA is single-stranded and contains deoxyribose and thymine
mRNA is double-stranded and contains ribose and thymine
questions.explanation: mRNA is a single strand of RNA nucleotides, each with the sugar ribose, and uracil replaces thymine. DNA is double-stranded, with deoxyribose and thymine.

questions.stem: A model of a tRNA molecule shows a folded single strand with a three-base sequence in one loop and an attachment site at one end. What are these two features?
options: A start codon that begins translation, and a site that binds RNA polymerase
A promoter that binds RNA polymerase, and a site that binds the next tRNA
An anticodon that pairs with a codon, and a site that binds a specific amino acid
A codon that pairs with the DNA, and a site that binds the small ribosome subunit
questions.explanation: Each tRNA has an anticodon that base-pairs with a complementary mRNA codon, and an attachment site at its 3' end that carries the amino acid matching that anticodon. Codons are on the mRNA, not the tRNA.

questions.stem: During transcription, which strand of DNA is used to build the mRNA, and how are the two related?
options: Both strands, each one producing half of the mRNA
The template strand, which has the same sequence as the mRNA
The template strand, which is complementary to the mRNA
The coding strand, which is complementary to the mRNA
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase reads the template strand and adds RNA nucleotides that are complementary to it. The coding strand therefore has the same sequence as the mRNA, except that it has T where the mRNA has U.

questions.stem: What is the role of RNA polymerase in polypeptide synthesis?
options: It removes introns from pre-mRNA before it leaves the nucleus
It joins free RNA nucleotides complementary to the template strand
It joins amino acids together with peptide bonds at the ribosome
It carries specific amino acids from the cytoplasm to the ribosome
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase unwinds a section of DNA and links free-floating RNA nucleotides that pair with the template strand, making mRNA. Peptide bonds are formed at the ribosome during translation, and tRNA carries the amino acids.

questions.stem: Where in a eukaryotic cell do transcription and translation take place?
options: Both take place in the nucleus, before the finished protein is exported
Transcription in the cytoplasm; translation inside the nucleolus
Transcription in the nucleus; translation at ribosomes in the cytoplasm
Transcription at ribosomes in the cytoplasm; translation in the nucleus
questions.explanation: DNA stays in the nucleus, so it is transcribed there; the mRNA then moves out through nuclear pores to ribosomes in the cytoplasm or on the rough endoplasmic reticulum for translation.

questions.stem: What is the role of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) in polypeptide synthesis?
options: It unwinds the DNA double helix at the start of transcription
It forms part of the ribosome and helps catalyse peptide bond formation
It carries the genetic code from the nucleus out to the ribosome
It brings specific amino acids to the ribosome using an anticodon
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are built of rRNA and proteins, and the rRNA catalyses the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids. Carrying the code is the job of mRNA, and bringing amino acids is the job of tRNA.

questions.stem: Which codon starts translation, and what does it code for?
options: AUG, which codes for methionine
UAA, which codes for methionine
AUG, which codes for no amino acid
UAG, which codes for leucine
questions.explanation: AUG is the start codon and also codes for methionine, so polypeptides begin with methionine. UAA and UAG are stop codons, which code for no amino acid.

questions.stem: During translation, the ribosome reaches the codon UAA on the mRNA. What happens next?
options: A release factor binds, and the polypeptide is freed from the ribosome
A tRNA carrying methionine binds, and a new polypeptide is started
The ribosome skips this codon and goes on to read the next triplet
RNA polymerase detaches from the template strand and stops copying
questions.explanation: UAA is a stop codon: no tRNA has a matching anticodon, so a release factor binds instead and the finished polypeptide is released. RNA polymerase belongs to transcription, which has already finished by this stage.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the roles of mRNA and tRNA?
options: mRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome; tRNA carries the code from DNA
mRNA catalyses peptide bonds; tRNA carries the code out of the nucleus
mRNA forms the ribosome; tRNA copies the code from the template strand
mRNA carries the code from DNA to the ribosome; tRNA brings amino acids to it
questions.explanation: mRNA is transcribed from the template strand and carries the sequence of codons to the ribosome. Each tRNA brings one amino acid and places it by pairing its anticodon with a codon.

questions.stem: A tRNA has the anticodon 3' UAC 5'. Which mRNA codon does it pair with, and which amino acid does it carry?
options: 5' CAU 3', and it carries histidine
5' AUG 3', and it carries methionine
5' UAC 3', and it carries tyrosine
5' ATG 3', and it carries methionine
questions.explanation: The codon is complementary and antiparallel to the anticodon, so 3' UAC 5' pairs with 5' AUG 3', the codon for methionine. Reading the anticodon itself as a codon gives UAC, tyrosine, which is the trap; ATG contains thymine, which RNA lacks.

questions.stem: The coding strand of an exon reads 5' ATG GCA TTC 3'. What is the sequence of the template strand?
options: 5' TAC CGT AAG 3'
3' ATG GCA TTC 5'
3' TAC CGT AAG 5'
3' UAC CGU AAG 5'
questions.explanation: The template strand is complementary and antiparallel to the coding strand, so each A pairs with T and each G with C, running 3' to 5'. It is DNA, so it contains T, not U.

questions.stem: The coding strand of an exon reads 5' ATG AAA TGG 3'. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this gene?
options: 3' UAC UUU ACC 5'
5' ATG AAA TGG 3'
5' AUG AAA UGG 3'
5' UAC UUU ACC 3'
questions.explanation: The mRNA is complementary to the template strand, so it has the same sequence as the coding strand with U in place of T. The sequences beginning UAC are complementary to the coding strand, which would be the case only if the coding strand were the template.

questions.stem: A template strand reads 3' TAC GGT CTT ATT 5'. Codons: AUG Met, CCA Pro, GAA Glu, UAA stop, GGU Gly, CUU Leu, UAC Tyr, AUU Ile. What polypeptide is made?
options: Met-Pro-Glu
Met-Gly-Leu
Tyr-Gly-Leu-Ile
Met-Pro-Glu-Ile
questions.explanation: The mRNA is complementary to the template: 5' AUG CCA GAA UAA 3', which gives Met-Pro-Glu and then a stop codon. Reading the template strand directly as if it were mRNA gives Tyr-Gly-Leu-Ile.

questions.stem: A short polypeptide reads Met-Trp-Lys. Methionine is coded only by AUG, tryptophan only by UGG, and lysine by AAA or AAG. How many different template strand sequences could code for it, ignoring the stop codon?
questions.explanation: Methionine and tryptophan each have one codon, while lysine has two, so there are 1 x 1 x 2 = 2 possible mRNA sequences and therefore 2 template sequences. This shows that the genetic code is degenerate.

questions.stem: During transcription, which base is added to the mRNA opposite an adenine on the template strand?
options: Guanine
Uracil
Thymine
Adenine
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with uracil in RNA. Thymine pairs with adenine only in DNA, so it is never added to mRNA.

questions.stem: What happens to the introns in pre-mRNA before the mRNA leaves the nucleus?
options: They are copied into tRNA molecules to provide new anticodons
They are cut out, and the exons are joined together
They are kept, and the exons are cut out and destroyed
They are translated into a short signal sequence of amino acids
questions.explanation: Introns are non-coding sequences removed by splicing, and the remaining exons are joined to form mature mRNA. Exons carry the coding sequence, so removing them would leave nothing to translate.

questions.stem: A pre-mRNA contains exons 1, 2, 3 and 4. In muscle cells the mature mRNA contains exons 1, 2 and 4; in nerve cells it contains exons 1, 3 and 4. What is this process and its result?
options: Crossing over, giving two different alleles of one gene in each tissue
Alternative splicing, giving the same protein in both kinds of cell
Point mutation of exons, giving two different genes in the two cells
Alternative splicing, giving two different proteins from one gene
questions.explanation: Joining different combinations of exons from one pre-mRNA is alternative splicing, and the two mRNAs code for different polypeptides. The DNA is the same in both cell types, so no mutation or crossing over is involved.

questions.stem: Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes but make many more different proteins than this. Which process best explains the difference?
options: Translation of introns as well as exons
Each codon coding for several amino acids
Reverse transcription of mRNA into new genes
Alternative splicing of exons in pre-mRNA
questions.explanation: Alternative splicing lets one gene produce several mRNAs and therefore several proteins. Each codon codes for only one amino acid, so the code is degenerate but not ambiguous.

questions.stem: A polypeptide chain coils into alpha helices and folds into beta pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between parts of the backbone. Which level of protein structure is this?
options: Secondary structure
Primary structure
Tertiary structure
Quaternary structure
questions.explanation: Alpha helices and beta pleated sheets are secondary structure. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, and tertiary structure is the overall 3D folding of a whole chain.

questions.stem: Haemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains, two alpha and two beta, each holding a haem group. Which level of structure describes how the four chains fit together?
options: Tertiary structure
Secondary structure
Primary structure
Quaternary structure
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains in one functional protein. The folding of each single chain into its 3D shape is tertiary structure.

questions.stem: In sickle cell disease, glutamic acid at one position in the beta chain of haemoglobin is replaced by valine. Why does this one change affect how the whole protein works?
options: The change removes the haem groups, so the molecule can no longer bind any oxygen
Valine cannot form peptide bonds, so the beta chain is never completely translated
The altered primary structure changes how chains fold and interact, so haemoglobin clumps
The extra amino acid lengthens each chain, so it no longer fits inside a red blood cell
questions.explanation: Primary structure determines how a chain folds and which surfaces it exposes. Valine is non-polar, so the altered haemoglobin molecules stick together at low oxygen and distort red blood cells. The amino acid is swapped, not added, and the haem groups remain.

questions.stem: Which protein is matched with its correct function?
options: Collagen: a structural protein that strengthens skin and tendons
Insulin: an enzyme that digests glucose in the small intestine
Haemoglobin: a hormone that signals cells to take up oxygen
Antibodies: transport proteins that carry fats in the blood
questions.explanation: Collagen is a fibrous structural protein in skin, tendons and bone. Insulin is a protein hormone, haemoglobin transports oxygen, and antibodies bind antigens in immune defence.

questions.stem: Why does an enzyme stop working after it is heated well above its optimum temperature?
options: Heat changes its amino acid sequence, turning it into a different enzyme
Heat makes its substrate molecules too large to enter the active site
Bonds holding its tertiary structure break, so its active site changes shape
Its peptide bonds break, so the amino acid sequence falls apart into pieces
questions.explanation: High temperature breaks the weaker hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the folded shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate. This is denaturation; the peptide bonds and the primary structure are left intact.

questions.stem: Some forms of albinism result from inheriting two faulty copies of the gene for tyrosinase, an enzyme needed to make melanin. Which sequence links the genotype to the phenotype?
options: Faulty enzyme, faulty mRNA, faulty DNA sequence, no melanin, pale skin
Faulty mRNA, faulty DNA sequence, no melanin, faulty enzyme, pale skin
Faulty DNA sequence, faulty mRNA, non-functional enzyme, no melanin, pale skin
Faulty DNA sequence, no melanin, faulty mRNA, non-functional enzyme, pale skin
questions.explanation: The DNA sequence is transcribed into mRNA, which is translated into the enzyme; an altered enzyme cannot catalyse melanin production, giving the phenotype. Information flows from DNA to mRNA to protein, never from protein back to DNA.

questions.stem: Hydrangea plants that are clones of each other flower blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil. What is the cause of the blue colour?
options: Acidic soil frees aluminium, which the plant takes up and which turns its pigment blue
Acidic soil changes the DNA sequence of the flower colour gene in the cells of the petals
Acidic soil kills the pink-flowered plants, so only those with alleles for blue survive
Acidic soil adds an extra copy of the chromosome carrying the blue colour allele
questions.explanation: In acidic soil aluminium becomes soluble, so the roots take it up and it combines with the petal pigment to give blue. The plants are genetically identical, so the colour difference is environmental, not a change in DNA.

questions.stem: A person's skin darkens after weeks of summer sun, and the tan fades over winter. Which explanation is correct?
options: UV light destroys melanin, so the skin cells then make a darker form of it
UV light permanently switches on the melanin genes in every cell of the body
UV light increases expression of genes for melanin; the tan is not inherited
UV light causes mutations in melanin genes, which pass to the person's children
questions.explanation: UV exposure stimulates melanocytes to make more melanin, an environmental effect on gene expression that reverses when exposure falls. Changes in skin cells are not passed on, because skin cells are not gametes.

questions.stem: In many sea turtle species, eggs incubated in warmer sand hatch mostly as females and those in cooler sand mostly as males. What does this show?
options: Female embryos carry extra genes that only allow them to survive in warm sand
Sex is set by X and Y chromosomes, and temperature only affects hatching rate
Incubation temperature affects which genes for sex development are expressed
Warmer sand causes mutations on the sex chromosomes of the developing embryos
questions.explanation: Sea turtles have temperature-dependent sex determination: they have no sex chromosomes, and the temperature during a sensitive stage of development changes which genes are expressed. The embryos' DNA is not altered.

questions.stem: A student grows bean seedlings from one packet, half in light and half in darkness, to test whether light affects expression of genes for chlorophyll. Which change would most improve the validity of the investigation?
options: Use seeds of a different species for the dark group to compare responses
Measure the seedlings' height instead of their colour after seven days
Keep temperature, water and soil the same and use many seedlings per group
Grow the dark group somewhere warmer so both groups grow at the same rate
questions.explanation: Validity requires that light is the only variable changed and that the measurement matches the aim, so other conditions must be controlled; many seedlings also reduce the effect of individual variation. Changing temperature or species adds new variables, and height does not measure chlorophyll.

questions.stem: Seedlings grown in darkness for a week are pale yellow. When moved into the light they turn green within a few days. What does this show about their genes for chlorophyll production?
options: Light caused new mutations that created genes for chlorophyll production
The seedlings lacked these genes until they were exposed to the light
Chlorophyll was made in the dark, and light only changed its colour
The genes were present all along and are expressed in response to light
questions.explanation: Every cell has the same genes; light acts as an environmental signal that switches on expression of genes for chlorophyll synthesis. Mutations are random and would not appear in every seedling within days.

questions.stem: What is microRNA (miRNA)?
options: A section of rRNA that holds the two ribosome subunits together
A short non-coding RNA that binds mRNA and reduces its translation
A short coding RNA that is translated into small peptide hormones
A form of tRNA that carries rare amino acids to the ribosome
questions.explanation: miRNAs are short RNAs that are not translated; they pair with complementary sequences in target mRNAs, blocking translation or causing the mRNA to be broken down. This regulates gene expression after transcription.

questions.stem: Researchers design a short interfering RNA (siRNA) complementary to the mRNA of a gene that makes a harmful protein. How could this treat a disease?
options: The siRNA leads to breakdown of the target mRNA, so less protein is made
The siRNA replaces the faulty gene in the DNA with a working copy
The siRNA binds the finished protein and changes its amino acid sequence
The siRNA inserts into the chromosome and blocks DNA replication
questions.explanation: In RNA interference the siRNA guides a protein complex to the matching mRNA, which is cut and degraded, silencing the gene. It acts on mRNA, so the DNA sequence of the gene is not changed.

questions.stem: A crop plant is engineered to make a double-stranded RNA matching an essential gene of an insect pest. Insects that feed on the plant die. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: The RNA blocks photosynthesis in the plant so the insect gets no nutrients
RNA interference silences the insect's gene by causing its mRNA to be degraded
The RNA is translated inside the insect into a toxic protein that poisons it
The RNA inserts into the insect's DNA and causes lethal frameshift mutations
questions.explanation: The insect's cells process the double-stranded RNA into short pieces that target the matching mRNA for destruction, so the essential protein is not made. The RNA is not translated, and it does not alter the insect's DNA.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an epigenetic mechanism?
options: Adding methyl groups to DNA near a gene's promoter
Substituting one base for another in an exon
Moving a chromosome section to a different chromosome
Doubling the full set of chromosomes in a cell
questions.explanation: Epigenetic changes alter gene expression without changing the DNA base sequence; DNA methylation is one such change and usually silences the gene. Base substitutions and translocations change the DNA itself, so they are mutations.

questions.stem: Genetically identical agouti mice can be yellow and obese or brown and lean. When pregnant mothers are fed a diet rich in methyl donors such as folic acid, more of their offspring are brown. Which explanation is best supported?
options: More DNA methylation activates the agouti gene, so more yellow pigment is made
More DNA methylation silences the agouti gene, so less yellow pigment is made
The diet caused mutations in the agouti gene that changed the offspring's DNA
Folic acid acts as a brown pigment that passes to the offspring in the womb
questions.explanation: Methyl donors increase methylation of DNA near the agouti gene, which silences it, giving brown, lean mice. The mice are genetically identical, so the difference is epigenetic rather than a mutation; methylation usually reduces, not increases, expression.

questions.stem: Rat pups that receive a lot of licking and grooming from their mothers have less methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) gene in the brain and cope better with stress as adults. Which explanation fits?
options: Licking changes the base sequence of the GR gene, creating a new dominant allele
More methylation increases GR expression, giving a much stronger stress response
Grooming removes the GR gene from brain cells, so stress hormones cannot act
Less methylation increases GR expression, giving better control of the stress response
questions.explanation: Less methylation leaves the GR gene more active, so more receptors are made and the stress response is switched off more effectively. This is an epigenetic effect of the environment; the DNA sequence is unchanged.

questions.stem: Why is polypeptide synthesis essential to all living things?
options: It makes proteins, such as enzymes, that determine cell structure and function
It makes the DNA that is copied and passed from parents to their offspring
It makes the glucose that provides energy for every process in the cell
It makes the phospholipids that form every membrane in the cell
questions.explanation: Polypeptide synthesis expresses genes as proteins: enzymes catalyse almost every reaction, and other proteins provide structure, transport, signalling and defence. DNA is made by replication, not by polypeptide synthesis.
